---
title: "Configuring a project"
subtitle: "A set of YAML files describes a basin, and each workflow reads its own"
---

The toolbox has no command-line interface. Everything a run needs comes from
**a set of configuration files**: one project file, plus one file per workflow.
You pass the *project* file to `--configfile` and it names the others.

Start from `config/templates/`, which annotates every option inline. Copy the
whole set — its header says which template becomes which file.
`test_case/project_config_baseline.yml` is a filled-in worked example, and
`test_case/project_config_rapid.yml` is the same basin sized for a quick
end-to-end run.

::: {.callout-important}
## Two path rules that catch people out

**`config_path:` resolves against the project file's own directory.** That is
what lets the set move as a unit: hand a colleague the folder and it runs
unchanged.

**Every other path resolves against the directory you run Snakemake from** (the
repository root). So `project_dir: test_case/test_rapid` means the same thing
wherever the config lives.

The two rules differ on purpose, and the second one is why: for real work, point
`project_dir` **outside the repository tree**. Run outputs are not source. The
in-repo `test_case/` projects are a development convention only.
:::

## Anatomy

### The project file

```yaml
schema_version: 2

project:
  project_dir: test_case/test_rapid
  catalog: config/catalogs/deltares_data.yml

basin:
  region: "{'subbasin': [9.666, 0.4476], 'uparea': 100}"
  resolution: 0.00833
  output_locations: test_case/test_data/output_locations.csv

climate:
  selected: era5
  window: {start: 2000, end: 2016}
  sources: [era5, chirps]

model:
  outvars: ['river discharge', 'actual evapotranspiration']

workflows:
  analyze_climate:
    enabled: true
    config_path: project_config_rapid_analyze_climate.yml
  build_model:
    enabled: true
    config_path: project_config_rapid_build_model.yml
  analyze_projections:
    enabled: true
    config_path: project_config_rapid_analyze_projections.yml
  run_stress_test:
    enabled: true
    config_path: project_config_rapid_run_stress_test.yml
```

**`schema_version: 2` is required.** It is checked before anything else, so a
config written for an older layout is refused with one message naming
[the migration note](../migration-config-shape.md) rather than a scatter of
complaints about individual keys.

- **`project.catalog`** names a **HydroMT data catalog**. Every dataset a run
  reads is registered in a catalog and referenced by name — data paths are never
  written directly into a workflow.
- **`basin.region`** is a HydroMT region specification. The example delineates
  the subbasin draining to a point at (9.666 °E, 0.4476 °N) with at least 100 km²
  of upstream area.
- **`climate.window`** is **inclusive calendar years**, and it sizes the
  historical climate store. The weather generator needs a floor of historical
  years to work from; a shorter window is refused at parse time rather than
  producing a quietly degraded stress test.
- **`climate.selected`** is the forcing dataset the model is driven with. Because
  the toolbox does no local calibration, this is the single most consequential
  setting in the set — which is what workflow 0 exists to inform.
  **`climate.sources`** is the full candidate list it compares; `selected` must
  be one of them.

Everything above `workflows:` is read by **more than one** workflow, and that is
the rule deciding what belongs here: a key two workflows read has to have one
home, or they can disagree about it. A key only one workflow reads is refused
here and belongs in that workflow's own file.

### The per-workflow files

Each `workflows.<name>` entry carries exactly two keys — `enabled:` and
`config_path:` — and nothing else. The settings live in the file it names:

```yaml
# project_config_rapid_build_model.yml
engine:
  build_config: config/defaults/wflow_build_model.yml
  waterbodies_config: config/defaults/wflow_update_waterbodies.yml
observations:
  river discharge: test_case/test_data/observations_timeseries.csv
simulation_window: {start: 2010, end: 2016}
```

`enabled:` must be a real boolean — unquoted `true`/`false`. A quoted `"true"`
or an integer `1` is rejected rather than guessed at, and a missing `enabled:` is
a hard error naming the absent key rather than a silent default.

`config_path:` is optional. A workflow you never run needs no file: delete the
key and set `enabled: false`. But a `config_path:` naming a file that is not
there is a hard parse error, on purpose, so a typo cannot pass as an empty
config.

::: {.callout-warning}
## `enabled: false` skips the run, it does not clean up after it

Disabling a workflow means the wrapper does not invoke it. Its previous outputs
are neither deleted nor refreshed, so an enabled downstream workflow consumes
whatever is already on disk. Staleness is yours to reason about.
:::

## Where the other configuration lives

| Directory | What it is | Do you edit it? |
|---|---|---|
| `config/catalogs/` | HydroMT data catalogs — the `-d` targets | Yes, to register a data source |
| `config/defaults/` | Build configs a rule actually reads (`wflow_build_model.yml`, `wflow_update_waterbodies.yml`, `weathergen_config.yml`) | Yes — changing one changes a run |
| `config/templates/` | Scaffolds you copy, including the set above | Copy, don't edit in place |
| `config/advanced_settings.yml` | Toolbox-wide limits and defaults, read for every project | Rarely |

`config/advanced_settings.yml` is **not** a `--configfile` target — it is read
once, for every project. It holds hard constraints no project config can relax
(the minimum number of historical years; the point at which a monthly relative
product stops being reportable), defaults a project config may override, and
external toolchain pins. Its schema is closed: an unknown key is rejected at
parse time rather than ignored.

::: {.callout-note}
## On Linux

Use the `*_linux.yml` variants of both the config set and the data catalog — the
data-catalog paths differ from Windows.
:::

## Naming an experiment

`experiment_name` in the stress-test file is optional. Left unset, the stress
test names the experiment after the project plus the date it was first created,
and **reuses** an existing dated experiment rather than minting today's date — so
incremental re-runs keep landing in the same place.

To pin a deliberate name (a scenario label, or a second experiment beside the
first), run this **once, before the first stress-test run**:

```bash
pixi run python scripts/suggest_experiment_name.py <your project file> --name dry_scenario
```

It reserves the directory atomically and writes the key back into your config,
leaving comments and layout intact. An existing value is never overwritten: the
experiment directory is what a completed run's outputs are addressed by, so
renaming it would strand them. Clear the key by hand to go back to the default.
